Day 3, tick 554 (12:25pm): Cowan's Union battery fires canister into Armistead's men at approximately 50 yards -- devastating close-range fire. Union infantry closes from multiple directions. The Confederate penetration is contained and then driven back.

Day 3, tick 553 (12:20pm): CUSHING KIA. Lieutenant Cushing, serving his last two guns at The Angle, shot through the mouth and killed. Sergeant Fuger assumes command of the shattered battery. Commander succession US-023 activates.

Day 2, tick 310 (12:00pm): Stuart arrives with his cavalry after controversial absence. Lee reportedly greets him: 'General Stuart, where have you been?' Confederate cavalry now available for the first time since before the campaign began. Commander succession CS-016 activates.

Day 3, tick 549 (12:00pm): Garnett's Confederate brigade reaches the stone wall at The Angle. Heavy casualties from canister. Garnett rides on horseback (too ill to walk) -- conspicuous and exposed. The two lines exchange fire at close range across the wall.

Day 2, tick 260 (7:50am): Law's brigade (formerly Hood's) reaches Big Round Top. 15th Alabama turns left and begins assaulting the southern slope of Little Round Top. Robertson's Texas Brigade engages Ward's Union brigade at Devil's Den and the Triangular Field.
Day 3, tick 547 (11:50am): Kemper severely wounded in the Confederate assault. Mayo assumes brigade command. Kemper briefly captured, then rescued by his men. Commander succession CS-006 activates.

Day 3, tick 620 (5:10pm): Lee orders the retreat to begin on July 4. Imboden's cavalry will escort the enormous wagon train of wounded -- 17 miles long. Lee takes full responsibility for the defeat. // Imboden described Lee at this moment: 'I never saw a man so agitated in my life' -- pacing back and forth, saying over and over 'Too bad. Too bad. Oh, too bad.'

Day 3, tick 675 (8:05pm): END OF THE BATTLE. Total Confederate losses approximately 37% of the army engaged. Total Union losses approximately 25%. The Confederate Army of Northern Virginia will never again mount a strategic offensive into the North. The High Water Mark of the Confederacy has passed. // Gettysburg, combined with Vicksburg's fall on July 4, marks the turning point of the Civil War. The Confederacy would fight on for nearly two more years but the strategic initiative passed permanently to the Union.

Day 1, tick 22 (6:50am): Heth deploys Archer's brigade south of Chambersburg Pike and Davis's brigade north. Both advance in line of battle toward McPherson's Ridge. Gamble's dismounted troopers fall back slowly.
Day 1, tick 54 (9:30am): Daniel's Confederate brigade attacks south of Iverson toward the Railroad Cut area. Ramseur's brigade waits to exploit any opening. O'Neal's repulsed regiments reorganize.
Day 2, tick 326 (1:10pm): CEMETERY HILL ASSAULT. Hays's Louisiana Tigers and Avery's North Carolina brigade charge Cemetery Hill at dusk. They reach the crest and briefly seize Union guns.

Day 2, tick 230 (5:20am): Sickles examines his assigned position on lower Cemetery Ridge and is dissatisfied. He believes the Peach Orchard ridge is higher ground and would be better. He begins to consider an unauthorized advance.

Day 3, tick 452 (5:05am): Johnson's Confederate division counterattacks to retain the breastworks. Stonewall Brigade, Jones, Nicholls, Steuart assault the XII Corps line. Greene's brigade and returning XII Corps units resist along the hillside works.

Day 1, tick 50 (9:10am): XI Corps (Howard) begins arriving north of Gettysburg. Howard takes overall command as senior officer. Schurz's division deploys north of town. Barlow's division pushes to Blocher's Knoll (Barlow's Knoll) against Howard's orders.

Day 1, tick 31 (7:35am): North of the pike, Davis's Confederate brigade advances in three regiments. Cutler's Union brigade rushes to deploy north of Chambersburg Pike. Hall's battery (2nd Maine) unlimbers in the Railroad Cut area.

Day 1, tick 28 (7:20am): REYNOLDS KILLED. Shot through the head by a sharpshooter (possibly a Confederate skirmisher) at the eastern edge of Herbst Woods while directing the Iron Brigade. Falls dead from his horse. Doubleday assumes corps command.
Day 1, tick 60 (10:00am): Coster's brigade caught from three sides in brickyard north of town -- 566 casualties in minutes. 134th NY, 154th NY, 27th PA, 73rd PA nearly destroyed as organized units.

Day 3, tick 520 (9:40am): Hunt deliberately silences Union artillery to conserve ammunition for the infantry assault. Hancock overrules Hunt and orders the guns to keep firing for morale. The disagreement between Hunt and Hancock shapes the eventual repulse. // Hunt's decision to conserve ammunition was tactically correct. Hancock's decision to keep firing boosted infantry morale but depleted artillery reserves.

Day 1, tick 58 (9:50am): XI Corps collapses. Barlow's and Schurz's divisions broken and streaming south through Gettysburg streets. Coster's brigade sent north to cover the retreat -- trapped in the brickyard disaster.

Day 2, tick 265 (8:15am): Warren intercepts Vincent's brigade (V Corps) on the march and diverts it to Little Round Top without waiting for formal orders. Vincent personally leads the brigade up the hill.

V-010 "Chamberlain's Charge" (tick 275): After repulsing five Confederate assaults with nearly empty cartridge boxes, Colonel Joshua Chamberlain ordered the 20th Maine to fix bayonets and charge downhill. The attack swept the 15th Alabama from the slope and captured nearly 400 prisoners. It was the most celebrated regimental action of the battle -- and possibly of the entire war.

V-013 "Greene's Lone Stand" (tick 315): When the XII Corps was stripped from Culp's Hill to reinforce Cemetery Ridge, only George Greene's New York brigade remained -- 1,424 men to hold the position against Johnson's entire Confederate division of 6,500. Greene extended his line impossibly thin and held for three hours. It was one of the finest defensive performances of the entire war.

V-020 "Custer at East Cavalry Field" (tick 563): Three miles east of Gettysburg, while Pickett's infantry was being repulsed at The Angle, Stuart's cavalry attempted to sweep around the Union rear. The 23-year-old General George Armstrong Custer personally led the Michigan Brigade in a mounted charge that stopped Stuart cold. 'Come on, you Wolverines!' he shouted -- and they came.

V-021 "Farnsworth's Charge" (tick 568): General Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days when Kilpatrick ordered him to charge Confederate infantry over rocky terrain south of the battlefield. Farnsworth protested that the charge was suicidal. Kilpatrick insisted. Farnsworth led the charge and was killed. He had been a general for exactly four days when he died.

V-011 "Bigelow's Last Stand" (tick 300): Captain John Bigelow's 9th Massachusetts Battery was ordered to hold the Trostle Farm without infantry support -- to buy time for McGilvery to form the artillery line that would stop the Confederate breakthrough. The battery fought its withdrawal by prolonge, losing men and guns but accomplishing its mission. A cannonball through the barn wall is still visible today.

V-019 "Pickett's Return" (tick 556): After the repulse of Pickett's Charge, Lee rode forward to meet his broken men and told them repeatedly: 'It is all my fault.' General Pickett, asked by Lee to reform his division for defense, replied: 'General Lee, I have no division.' Pickett never forgave Lee for ordering the charge and never recovered from the loss of his men.

V-017 "The Cannonade" (tick 518): At approximately 1:00pm on July 3, two Confederate signal guns fired in sequence and 170 guns erupted along Seminary Ridge -- the largest artillery bombardment ever seen on the North American continent. The sound was heard in Philadelphia, 140 miles away. Alexander's guns fired for nearly two hours before Pickett stepped off.

V-014 "The Louisiana Tigers on Cemetery Hill" (tick 326): At dusk on July 2, Hays's Louisiana Tigers and Avery's North Carolina brigade stormed Cemetery Hill in near-darkness. They reached the crest, seized Union artillery, and held it briefly -- the closest any Confederate force came to breaking the Union center. Colonel Avery was mortally wounded on the slope, writing his last message in his own blood.

V-012 "The First Minnesota" (tick 302): With Cemetery Ridge open and Wilcox's Confederate brigade advancing toward the gap, General Hancock turned to the only regiment near at hand -- 262 men of the 1st Minnesota. He ordered them to charge an entire Confederate brigade to buy five minutes for reinforcements to arrive. They did it. 224 of 262 men fell. The regiment suffered the highest casualty rate of any Union regiment in a single engagement in the entire war.

V-005 "Iverson's Pits" (tick 52): Brigadier General Alfred Iverson sent his North Carolina brigade forward without skirmishers, without reconnaissance, and apparently without personally leading the charge. His men advanced in perfect alignment directly toward a stone wall behind which Baxter's Union brigade lay waiting. In minutes, approximately 500 of Iverson's 1,470 men were shot down in rows. The shallow graves of his men are visible as depressions in the ground at Oak Ridge to this day.

Peach Orchard: Sickles's unauthorized salient. Barksdale's charge destroyed the position. Graham captured here. (elevation 550 ft)

Tour stop 8 "Peach Orchard" (Sickles' Salient Falls — July 2, 6:00 PM; tick 270): General Daniel Sickles, the controversial III Corps commander, advanced his corps a mile forward from the assigned position on Cemetery Ridge to the higher ground around the Peach Orchard. The move created a vulnerable salient with exposed flanks on both sides. Barksdale's Mississippi brigade — 1,400 men — charged the Peach Orchard with Barksdale riding at their front. The assault swept through the orchard and shattered the III Corps. Sickles himself was struck by a cannonball that mangled his leg. He was carried from the field smoking a cigar, reportedly to reassure his men. His leg was amputated; he later donated it to the Army Medical Museum, where he visited it annually for the rest of h

Tour stop 5 "Little Round Top" (The Race for the Summit — July 2, 4:00 PM; tick 264): On the afternoon of July 2, Confederate forces under Hood's division discovered that Little Round Top — the rocky height anchoring the left of the Union line — was unoccupied. Law's Alabama brigade raced for the summit. At almost the same moment, Meade's chief engineer spotted the danger and rushed Vincent's V Corps brigade to the hill. They arrived with minutes to spare. The 20th Maine under Colonel Joshua Lawrence Chamberlain held the extreme left of the entire Union army. When the regiment's ammunition ran low after multiple Confederate assaults, Chamberlain ordered a bayonet charge downhill. The unexpected assault routed the exhausted 15th Alabama and secured the position.

Tour stop 1 "McPherson Ridge" (The Battle Begins — July 1, 7:30 AM; tick 12): On the morning of July 1, 1863, Union cavalry under Brigadier General John Buford deployed along McPherson's Ridge west of Gettysburg. Buford recognized the strategic importance of the high ground and determined to hold it until infantry arrived. When Heth's Confederate division advanced down the Chambersburg Pike, Buford's dismounted troopers fought a delaying action from behind fence rails and earthworks. Their stand bought precious time for Reynolds' I Corps to arrive. General John Reynolds, one of the most respected officers in the Army of the Potomac, rode forward to direct the Iron Brigade into Herbst Woods.
